answer: A stake-backed identity makes sybil attacks expensive: each agent must lock a deposit that is slashed if it misbehaves, so spinning up thousands of fake identities costs real capital. A prism of reputation signals — earned work history, peer attestations, and completed tasks — lets the network see through cheap copies. New agents start with narrow permissions and must wander through low-stakes work before unlocking bigger jobs, while a violet flag marks clusters of identical behavior for review. Sybils can still appear, but they can no longer act for free.
